name: verify-loop
description: Verify Loop: one place to verify a change or claim. It writes a check that can fail, loops until the check passes, keeps the proof, and returns a fixed answer (verdict, VERIFY: line, observed rejection, gaps). Users, skills and agents can all call it. Create mode generates a project /verify skill; maintain mode keeps it honest as the app changes. Also ships feature-map (manual-only): a FEATURES.md of every feature, its entry points and traces, checked against the code and linked to VERIFY.md. And latent-audit (manual-only): dead code removed without breaking anything, in plain words: only code that is truly never loaded or called is deleted (not code loaded by a name built at runtime, a config or schedule, a plugin or an entry point), every command is rerun after, every suspect left gets a dead, live or watch verdict kept for the next session, and imports that point up a declared layer order are listed. And wire-check (manual-only): is code connected to the running system, in plain words: every way in is run, a piece counts as wired only if a real way in reached it, each piece nothing reached gets a verdict naming its first broken link with file:line, and a component you connect keeps a check in the suite that fails when the wiring breaks. And debug-protocol (manual-only): the root cause proven both ways, the failure reproduced on demand and gone with only the cause taken out, then the tree left as it was or fixed at the cause and held by a check that fails with the cause put back. And structure-gate (manual-only): is it spaghetti, measured? The share of code a parser actually entered comes first, every region no parser entered (code in a string, a language with no parser here) gets a counted reading or UNKNOWN, every finding gets its cost, and a `no` verdict is refused over code no linter or test can reach. And threat-model (manual-only): what an attacker can make the system do, worst first, in plain words: every way in is attacked or shown to have nothing behind it, each attack is run and kept as a test the suite runs, and a fix passes now and fails again with the change taken out. And evolve-maintain (manual-only): change a running system without breaking it, in plain words: what the commands users and jobs run print and write is kept before the edit, every reader of a changed name is exercised or explained, and any difference after the change that was not asked for is fixed. The tree as it was is kept and the commands users and jobs run are recorded on it, every function or config line that reads a name the change touched must be entered by a recorded run or given a reason, and every recorded command must print and write on the changed tree what it did before, unless the difference is one the user asked for. And perf-optimize (manual-only): make it measurably faster, in plain words: time the work on the code as it was at two sizes and find where the time goes from runs; a change keeps the output the same, beats the noise and aims at what the measurement showed, and a check left in the suite fails when the gain is taken out. And safe-release (manual-only): deploy, or change stored data, with a way back that was run, not guessed, in plain words: forward, its rerun and the way back are rehearsed on a copy of the live data, today's code runs on the migrated copy (the deploy window and a code-only revert), the data after the way back is compared row for row, each loss is named with the step that causes it, and the live data is never written. And arch-design (manual-only): could the architecture be better? Where the structure costs the user, counted, shown as before/after pictures with the chain behind each problem, the top move written out with its landing steps, proof and door, the store or seam it is not adding, and a stop to ask which move to explore before anything changes. And blast-radius (manual-only): what a change breaks outside its diff, in plain words: every consumer of what the diff changed (callers, and renamed keys, fields, columns, env vars and flags found by literal name) gets a breaks, cleared or unknown verdict with a citation, and the change is called safe only when the one fact it is safe because of has a proof that passes on the change and fails with that fact broken. And mistake-proof (manual-only): make a mistake agents keep repeating impossible, in plain words: repeats are found in the history (reverts, reverted changes brought back, fixes naming an earlier commit, workaround comments) and the operator's corrections, each with two real pieces of evidence; each is fixed at the strongest level that works, architecture down to docs, saying why stronger ones did not; a check fails on the commit with the mistake and passes now, in CI when there is CI; and each rule in the agent file names what enforces it. And untangle (manual-only): untangle where the history says changes hurt. Files ranked by commits and fix commits, and pairs that keep changing together, each get a target or a reason to skip; the tests are recorded on the committed tree first and every test already red is classified env, stale or bug (with its file:line); every changed file serves a target, every move's guard passes now and fails on the committed tree, and no test that was green goes red. And cleanup (manual-only): clear what agents leave behind, in plain words: each piece of mess (leftover copies, litter, orphaned modules, dead and duplicate functions, unused imports, debug leftovers, commented-out code, change-log comments) is removed, merged, kept with a reason or reported by file:line; no test that passed fails, no fewer tests run, a deleted file is named nowhere, swallowed errors, stubs and hard-coded answers are named before any fix that changes behavior, and each run's record lets the next one say what is new and what came back. And checkup (manual-only): how well a codebase is structured, and what to fix first. One report over the git-tracked files in eight sections (easy to find things, one change in one place, dependencies one way, deep modules, one way per job, logic apart from I/O, dead code, tests that can fail), each measured by the sibling helpers or said `not checked`; every finding is weighted by the commits and fix commits of its files, so a tangle nobody changes ranks below files that keep changing together; each top finding needs a cost citing a commit that touched it or a reason it is right, and the three fixes are the costed findings, highest weight first. And dependency-health (manual-only): what the dependencies owe. Known holes (OSV.dev or a given advisories file, direct and pulled in by others, with what pulls them in), end-of-life runtimes, lockfiles out of step with their manifest, packages nothing uses (and ones used without an import), exact pins with no reason; an ecosystem it could not check is listed as not checked, never healthy; done is refused while a high finding is neither fixed nor accepted with a reason and a date, a test that passed fails, fewer tests run or a manifest changed without its lockfile, and the record lets the next run say what is new and which acceptances are due again. And state-machines (manual-only): the state machines a codebase never declared, in plain words: every write and check of a status field or flag is accounted for by file:line, each value checked but never set and each state nothing leaves gets a verdict, each bug is proven by a test that fails on the code as it was, and each machine is drawn as a diagram. And test-diet (manual-only): tests shorter to read and faster to run, with nothing lost, in plain words: setup repeated across tests, slow tests and their cause, and tests that only check mocks are slimmed or kept with a reason; the old suite's times and the planted bugs it catches are recorded first; no app file changes, and the new tests pass, are no longer and no slower, and catch every planted bug the old ones caught. The install runs no hooks.
